verses.zh: 当暗拉非作示拿王，亚略作以拉撒王，基大老玛作以拦王，提达作戈印王的时候，
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] Amraphel king of Shinar,[NOTE:2] Arioch king of Ellasar, Kedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations[NOTE:3]
notes: The sentence begins with the temporal indicator וַיְהִי (vayehi) followed by “in the days of.”
Shinar (also in v. 9) is the region of Babylonia.
Or “king of Goyim.” The Hebrew term גּוֹיִם (goyim) means “nations,” but a number of modern translations merely transliterate the Hebrew (cf. NEB, NIV11 “Goyim”; NRSV, NIV84 “Goiim”).

verses.zh: 他们都攻打所多玛王比拉、蛾摩拉王比沙、押玛王示纳、洗扁王善以别，和比拉王；比拉就是琐珥。
verses.en: went to war[NOTE:1] against Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboyim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar).[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “made war.”sn Went to war. The conflict here reflects international warfare in the Early and Middle Bronze periods. The countries operated with overlords and vassals. Kings ruled over city states, or sometimes a number of city states (i.e., nations). Due to their treaties, when one went to war, those confederate with him joined him in battle. It appears here that it is Kedorlaomer’s war because the western city states have rebelled against him (meaning they did not send products as tribute to keep him from invading them).

On the geographical background of vv. 1-2 see J. P. Harland, “Sodom and Gomorrah,” The Biblical Archaeologist Reader, 1:41-75; and D. N. Freedman, “The Real Story of the Ebla Tablets, Ebla and the Cities of the Plain,” BA 41 (1978): 143-64.

verses.zh: 这五王都在西订谷会合；西订谷就是盐海。
verses.en: These last five kings[NOTE:1] joined forces[NOTE:2] in the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea).[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “all these,” referring only to the last five kings named. The referent has been specified as “these last five kings” in the translation for clarity.
The Hebrew verb used here means “to join together; to unite; to be allied.” It stresses close associations, especially of friendships, marriages, or treaties.
The Salt Sea is the older name for the Dead Sea.

verses.zh: 他们已经事奉基大老玛十二年，到十三年就背叛了。
verses.en: For twelve years[NOTE:1] they had served Kedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year[NOTE:2] they rebelled.[NOTE:3]
notes: The sentence simply begins with “twelve years”; it serves as an adverbial accusative giving the duration of their bondage.
This is another adverbial accusative of time.

The story serves as a foreshadowing of the plight of the kingdom of Israel later. Eastern powers came and forced the western kingdoms into submission. Each year, then, they would send tribute east—to keep them away. Here, in the thirteenth year, they refused to send the tribute (just as later Hezekiah rebelled against Assyria). And so in the fourteenth year the eastern powers came to put them down again. This account from Abram’s life taught future generations that God can give victory over such threats—that people did not have to live in servitude to tyrants from the east.

verses.zh: 十四年，基大老玛和同盟的王都来在亚特律・加宁，杀败了利乏音人，在哈麦杀败了苏西人，在沙微・基列亭杀败了以米人，
verses.en: In the fourteenth year, Kedorlaomer and the kings who were his allies came and defeated[NOTE:1] the Rephaites in Ashteroth Karnaim, the Zuzites in Ham, the Emites in Shaveh Kiriathaim,
notes: The Hebrew verb נָכָה (nakhah) means “to attack, to strike, to smite.” In this context it appears that the strike was successful, and so a translation of “defeated” is preferable.

verses.zh: 在何利人的西珥山杀败了何利人，一直杀到靠近旷野的伊勒・巴兰。
verses.en: and the Horites in their hill country of Seir, as far as El Paran, which is near the desert.[NOTE:1]
notes: The line of attack ran down the eastern side of the Jordan Valley into the desert, and then turned and came up the valley to the cities of the plain.

verses.zh: 他们回到安・密巴，就是加低斯，杀败了亚玛力全地的人，以及住在哈洗逊・他玛的亚摩利人。
verses.en: Then they attacked En Mishpat (that is, Kadesh) again,[NOTE:1] and they conquered all the territory of the Amalekites, as well as the Amorites who were living in Hazezon Tamar.
notes: Heb “they returned and came to En Mishpat (that is, Kadesh).” The two verbs together form a verbal hendiadys, the first serving as the adverb: “they returned and came” means “they came again.” Most English translations do not treat this as a hendiadys, but translate “they turned back” or something similar. Since in the context, however, “came again to” does not simply refer to travel but an assault against the place, the present translation expresses this as “attacked…again.”

verses.zh: 于是所多玛王、蛾摩拉王、押玛王、洗扁王，和比拉王（比拉就是琐珥）都出来，在西订谷摆阵，与他们交战，
verses.en: Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboyim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) went out and prepared for battle. In the Valley of Siddim they met[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “against.”

verses.zh: 就是与以拦王基大老玛、戈印王提达、示拿王暗拉非、以拉撒王亚略交战；乃是四王与五王交战。
verses.en: Kedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of nations,[NOTE:1] Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar. Four kings fought against[NOTE:2] five.
notes: Or “Goyim.” See the note on the word “nations” in 14:1.
The Hebrew text has simply “against.” The word “fought” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 西订谷有许多石漆坑。所多玛王和蛾摩拉王逃跑，有掉在坑里的，其余的人都往山上逃跑。
verses.en: Now the Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits.[NOTE:1] When the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, they fell into them,[NOTE:2] but some survivors[NOTE:3] fled to the hills.[NOTE:4]
notes: The word for “tar” (or “bitumen”) occurs earlier in the story of the building of the tower in Babylon (see Gen 11:3).tn Heb “Now the Valley of Siddim [was] pits, pits of tar.” This parenthetical disjunctive clause emphasizes the abundance of tar pits in the area through repetition of the noun “pits.”
Or “they were defeated there.” After a verb of motion the Hebrew particle שָׁם (sham) with the directional he (שָׁמָּה, shammah) can mean “into it, therein” (BDB 1027 s.v. שָׁם).
Heb “the rest.”
The reference to the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah must mean the kings along with their armies. Most of them were defeated in the valley, but some of them escaped to the hills.

verses.zh: 四王就把所多玛和蛾摩拉所有的财物，并一切的粮食都掳掠去了；
verses.en: The four victorious kings[NOTE:1] took all the possessions and food of Sodom and Gomorrah and left.
notes: Heb “they”; the referent (the four victorious kings, see v. 9) has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 又把亚伯兰的侄儿罗得和罗得的财物掳掠去了。当时罗得正住在所多玛。
verses.en: They also took Abram’s nephew[NOTE:1] Lot and his possessions when[NOTE:2] they left, for Lot[NOTE:3] was living in Sodom.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “Lot the son of his brother.”
Heb “and.”
Heb “he”; the referent (Lot) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
This disjunctive clause is circumstantial/causal, explaining that Lot was captured because he was living in Sodom at the time.

verses.zh: 有一个逃出来的人告诉希伯来人亚伯兰；亚伯兰正住在亚摩利人幔利的橡树那里。幔利和以实各并亚乃都是弟兄，曾与亚伯兰联盟。
verses.en: A fugitive[NOTE:1] came and told Abram the Hebrew.[NOTE:2] Now Abram was living by the oaks[NOTE:3] of Mamre the Amorite, the brother[NOTE:4] of Eshcol and Aner. (All these were allied by treaty[NOTE:5] with Abram.)[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “the fugitive.” The article carries a generic force or indicates that this fugitive is definite in the mind of the speaker.

E. A. Speiser (Genesis [AB], 103) suggests that part of this chapter came from an outside source since it refers to Abram the Hebrew. That is not impossible, given that the narrator likely utilized traditions and genealogies that had been collected and transmitted over the years. The meaning of the word “Hebrew” has proved elusive. It may be related to the verb “to cross over,” perhaps meaning “immigrant.” Or it might be derived from the name of Abram’s ancestor Eber (see Gen 11:14-16).
Or “terebinths.”
Or “a brother”; or “a relative”; or perhaps “an ally.”

Heb “possessors of a treaty with.” Since it is likely that the qualifying statement refers to all three (Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner) the words “all these” have been supplied in the translation to make this clear.
This parenthetical disjunctive clause explains how Abram came to be living in their territory, but it also explains why they must go to war with Abram.

verses.zh: 亚伯兰听见他侄儿被掳去，就率领他家里生养的精练壮丁三百一十八人，直追到但，
verses.en: When Abram heard that his nephew[NOTE:1] had been taken captive, he mobilized[NOTE:2] his 318 trained men who had been born in his household, and he pursued the invaders[NOTE:3] as far as Dan.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “his brother,” by extension, “relative.” Here and in v. 16 the more specific term “nephew” has been used in the translation for clarity. Lot was the son of Haran, Abram’s brother (Gen 11:27).

The verb וַיָּרֶק (vayyareq) is a rare form, probably related to the word רֵיק (req, “to be empty”). If so, it would be a very figurative use: “he emptied out” (or perhaps “unsheathed”) his men. The LXX has “mustered” (cf. NEB). E. A. Speiser (Genesis [AB], 103-4) suggests reading with Smr a verb diq, cognate with Akkadian deku, “to mobilize” troops. If this view is accepted, one must assume that a confusion of the Hebrew letters ד (dalet) and ר (resh) led to the error in the traditional Hebrew text. These two letters are easily confused in all phases of ancient Hebrew script development. The present translation is based on this view.
The words “the invaders” have been supplied in the translation for clarification.

The use of the name Dan reflects a later perspective. The Danites did not migrate to this northern territory until centuries later (see Judg 18:29). Furthermore Dan was not even born until much later. By inserting this name a scribe has clarified the location of the region.

verses.zh: 便在夜间，自己同仆人分队杀败敌人，又追到大马士革北边的何把，
verses.en: Then, during the night,[NOTE:1] Abram[NOTE:2] divided his forces[NOTE:3] against them and defeated them. He chased them as far as Hobah, which is north[NOTE:4] of Damascus.
notes: The Hebrew text simply has “night” as an adverbial accusative.
Heb “he”; the referent (Abram) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “he divided himself…he and his servants.”
Heb “left.” Directions in ancient Israel were given in relation to the east rather than the north.

verses.zh: 将被掳掠的一切财物夺回来，连他侄儿罗得和他的财物，以及妇女、人民也都夺回来。
verses.en: He retrieved all the stolen property.[NOTE:1] He also brought back his nephew Lot and his possessions, as well as the women and the rest of[NOTE:2] the people.
notes: The word “stolen” is supplied in the translation for clarification.
The phrase “the rest of “ has been supplied in the translation for clarification.

verses.zh: 亚伯兰杀败基大老玛和与他同盟的王回来的时候，所多玛王出来，在沙微谷迎接他；沙微谷就是王谷。
verses.en: After Abram[NOTE:1] returned from defeating Kedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram[NOTE:2] in the Valley of Shaveh (known as the King’s Valley).[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Abram) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “him”; the referent (Abram) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The King’s Valley is possibly a reference to what came to be known later as the Kidron Valley.

verses.zh: 又有撒冷王麦基洗德带着饼和酒出来迎接；他是至高　神的祭司。
verses.en: Melchizedek king of Salem[NOTE:1] brought out bread and wine. (Now he was the priest of the Most High God.)[NOTE:2]
notes: Salem is traditionally identified as the Jebusite stronghold of old Jerusalem. Accordingly, there has been much speculation about its king. Though some have identified him with the preincarnate Christ or with Noah’s son Shem, it is far more likely that Melchizedek was a Canaanite royal priest whom God used to renew the promise of the blessing to Abram, perhaps because Abram considered Melchizedek his spiritual superior. But Melchizedek remains an enigma. In a book filled with genealogical records he appears on the scene without a genealogy and then disappears from the narrative. In Ps 110 the Lord declares that the Davidic king is a royal priest after the pattern of Melchizedek.

The parenthetical disjunctive clause significantly identifies Melchizedek as a priest as well as a king.sn It is his royal priestly status that makes Melchizedek a type of Christ: He was identified with Jerusalem, superior to the ancestor of Israel, and both a king and a priest. Unlike the normal Canaanites, this man served “God Most High” (אֵל עֶלְיוֹן, ʾel ʿelyon)—one sovereign God, who was the creator of all the universe. Abram had in him a spiritual brother.

verses.zh: 他为亚伯兰祝福，说：「愿天地的主、至高的　神赐福与亚伯兰！
verses.en: He blessed Abram, saying, “Blessed be Abram by[NOTE:1] the Most High God, Creator[NOTE:2] of heaven and earth.[NOTE:3]
notes: The preposition ל (lamed) introduces the agent after the passive participle.

Some translate “possessor of heaven and earth” (cf. NASB). But cognate evidence from Ugaritic indicates that there were two homonymic roots קָנָה (qanah), one meaning “to create” (as in Gen 4:1) and the other “to obtain, to acquire, to possess.” While “possessor” would fit here, “Creator” is the more likely due to the collocation with “heaven and earth.”
The terms translated “heaven” and “earth” are both objective genitives after the participle in construct.

verses.zh: 至高的　神把敌人交在你手里，是应当称颂的！」亚伯兰就把所得的拿出十分之一来，给麦基洗德。
verses.en: Worthy of praise is[NOTE:1] the Most High God, who delivered[NOTE:2] your enemies into your hand.” Abram gave Melchizedek[NOTE:3] a tenth of everything.
notes: Heb “blessed be.” For God to be “blessed” means that he is praised. His reputation is enriched in the world as his name is praised.

Who delivered. The Hebrew verb מִגֵּן (miggen, “delivered”) foreshadows the statement by God to Abram in Gen 15:1, “I am your shield” (מָגֵן, magen). Melchizedek provided a theological interpretation of Abram’s military victory.
Heb “him”; the referent (Melchizedek) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 所多玛王对亚伯兰说：「你把人口给我，财物你自己拿去吧！」
verses.en: Then the king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people and take the possessions for yourself.”

verses.zh: 亚伯兰对所多玛王说：「我已经向天地的主―至高的　神耶和华起誓：
verses.en: But Abram replied to the king of Sodom, “I raise my hand[NOTE:1] to the Lord, the Most High God, Creator of heaven and earth, and vow[NOTE:2]
notes: Abram takes an oath, raising his hand as a solemn gesture. The translation understands the perfect tense as having an instantaneous nuance: “Here and now I raise my hand.”
The words “and vow” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarification.

verses.zh: 凡是你的东西，就是一根线、一根鞋带，我都不拿，免得你说：『我使亚伯兰富足！』
verses.en: that I will take nothing[NOTE:1] belonging to you, not even a thread or the strap of a sandal. That way you can never say, ‘It is I[NOTE:2] who made Abram rich.’
notes: The oath formula is elliptical, reading simply: “…if I take.” It is as if Abram says, “[May the Lord deal with me] if I take,” meaning, “I will surely not take.” The positive oath would add the negative adverb and be the reverse: “[God will deal with me] if I do not take,” meaning, “I certainly will.”
The Hebrew text adds the independent pronoun (“I”) to the verb form for emphasis.

verses.zh: 只有仆人所吃的，并与我同行的亚乃、以实各、幔利所应得的分，可以任凭他们拿去。」
verses.en: I will take nothing[NOTE:1] except compensation for what the young men have eaten.[NOTE:2] As for the share of the men who went with me—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre—let them take their share.”
notes: The words “I will take nothing” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “except only what the young men have eaten.”
